s: A hearing before the deprivation is the norm.
Prompt action is necessary, as with summary seizure of misbranded drugs or contaminated food, or emergency suspension (FDIC v. Mallen).
The deprivation is random and unauthorized, so the state cannot predict it.
An adequate post-deprivation tort remedy then satisfies due process (Parratt v. Taylor, 1981; Hudson v. Palmer, 1984).
This does not apply when the deprivation follows established state procedure (Logan v. Zimmerman Brush, 1982).
The required process varies by context.
In schools, a short suspension requires only informal notice and an opportunity to explain (Goss v. Lopez, 1975).
Paddling requires no prior hearing, because tort remedies suffice (Ingraham v. Wright, 1977).
In civil commitment, the standard of proof must be clear and convincing evidence (Addington v. Texas, 1979).
Parental rights termination likewise requires clear and convincing evidence (Santosky).
